question: An analyst is presenting a Claude-assisted workflow to sceptical senior stakeholders next week. Which two things should the presentation include? Select two.
options: A) A comparison of technical benchmark scores across each of the underlying model tiers.
B) A claim that Claude will not make any factual errors once all its instructions are written well.
C) A specific, measured example of what the workflow improved during the pilot it ran on.
D) Where a human still reviews the output, and why that review step has been kept in place.
E) A promise that the workflow removes any need to check the output from this point onward.
correct_answers: C) A specific, measured example of what the workflow improved during the pilot it ran on.
D) Where a human still reviews the output, and why that review step has been kept in place.
explanations: Incorrect. Benchmark scores are not what a business audience needs, and they say nothing about this workflow's value.
Incorrect. Good instructions reduce error but do not eliminate it, so this claim is false and will damage trust later.
Correct. A measured pilot result is concrete evidence of value rather than an assertion stakeholders are asked to take on trust.
Correct. Naming where human review remains, and why, is honest limitation-setting and is what makes the value claim credible.
Incorrect. Promising that checking is no longer needed oversells the tool and sets the expectation that will break first.
